title: How Much Bark Per Pound of Fibre
summary: Start at fifty to a hundred per cent of the dry fibre weight: half a pound of bark to a pound of wool for a mid shade, a pound to a pound for a deep one. Weigh the fibre dry, before wetting, and write the ratio down.
body: Every ratio in natural dyeing is a percentage of the **dry weight of the fibre**, weighed before it is wetted. Wet wool holds several times its own weight in water, so weighing it damp makes every number afterwards meaningless.
## Working ratios

| Depth wanted | Bark as % of fibre weight | For 1 lb of wool |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Pale, tint | 25 to 40% | 4 to 6 oz |
| Mid shade | 50 to 75% | 8 to 12 oz |
| Deep | 100% | 1 lb |
| As dark as the fibre will take | 125% and a second bath | 1 lb 4 oz |

Past about a hundred and twenty-five per cent the bath holds more colour than the fibre can pick up. The surplus goes down the drain or into a [second bath](/blog/getting-a-second-and-third-bath-from-one-batch), which is the sensible use for it.
## Water volume changes nothing about depth

This is the point that takes longest to believe. Depth comes from the ratio of colour to fibre, not from how concentrated the liquid looks. A pound of bark in two gallons and a pound in five give much the same shade — the five-gallon pot just lets the fibre move.
What volume does decide is **evenness**. Fibre packed into too little water dyes in patches where it touched itself. Use enough water that a skein can be lifted and turned without force.
## Cut matters as much as quantity

Powder puts far more surface area into the water than the same weight of shredded bark, so it loads a bath faster and reaches a usable depth sooner. Shredded bark works more slowly and is easier to strain. The same weight of either ends up in roughly the same place given time; the powder simply gets there first. See [why particle size changes everything in a dye pot](/blog/why-particle-size-changes-everything-in-a-dye-pot).
## Write it down

Bark from different harvests varies, and so does your water. A ratio that gave the right shade in March will not repeat in September unless you recorded it. Note the dry fibre weight, the bark weight, the cut, the temperature, the time and the water — the last one surprises people, because hard water shifts this colour.
For small quantities and test pots, see [testing a dye before you commit a fleece](/blog/testing-a-dye-before-you-commit-a-fleece).

title: Using pH to Steer the Shade
summary: A small pH shift moves this colour a long way: acid pushes it towards red and rust, alkali towards violet and grey. Change one thing at a time, add it a teaspoon at a time, and keep wool between pH 5 and 8 or the fibre itself starts to suffer.
body: Once your temperature is reliable, pH is the most useful control you have. It is also the fastest way to ruin a bath, because the shift happens in seconds and cannot be un-shifted cleanly.
## Which direction does what

| Adjustment | What to add | Where the colour goes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| More acid | White vinegar, citric acid | Warmer — towards red, rust, terracotta |
| Neutral | Nothing | The bath's own purple to maroon |
| More alkali | Soda ash, washing soda | Cooler — towards violet, then grey |

The tannins in this bark are sensitive enough that half a teaspoon of soda ash in a small pot is visible. Test the liquid on a scrap of the same fibre before committing, because the shade in the pot is not the shade on the wool.
## The safe range for the fibre

Colour is not the only thing pH affects. **Wool and silk are protein fibres and they do not tolerate alkali**: above about pH 9 the fibre turns harsh and slippery, loses strength, and no rinse brings it back. Keep protein fibres between pH 5 and 8.
Cotton and linen are far more tolerant of alkali and rather less tolerant of strong acid. See [wool, silk, cotton and linen in the same bath](/blog/wool-silk-cotton-and-linen-in-the-same-bath).
## How to add it

1. Dissolve the acid or alkali in a cup of water first. Never tip dry soda ash onto fibre.
2. Lift the fibre out of the pot.
3. Stir the adjustment in, a teaspoon at a time, and measure.
4. Put the fibre back and give it ten minutes before judging.
Adding anything to a pot with fibre in it is how you get a streak exactly where the liquid landed.
## Measuring

Paper strips are enough for this work: you are looking for a range, not a decimal place. Test your tap water before you blame anything else, since water out of the tap is often already at pH 7.5 to 8.5, and hard water will pull the shade towards grey on its own.
## Order of operations
Get temperature right, then ratio, then pH, then [iron](/blog/iron-as-a-modifier-how-far-to-go). Changing two at once teaches you nothing about which one moved the colour.

title: Iron as a Modifier, and How Far to Go
summary: Iron darkens and greys a tannin colour in seconds, taking purple to slate and brown to charcoal. Keep it to one or two per cent of the fibre weight, use a separate pot, dip rather than simmer, and pull the fibre while it still looks too light.
body: Iron and tannin react. That reaction is the oldest black in textile history, and on a tannin-rich bark it works so fast that the usual advice is not about how to do it but about how to stop in time.
## What it does

Ferrous sulfate — copperas, or iron sulfate — combines with tannin to make a dark grey-black complex. On a bark bath the result is a genuine slate, charcoal or near-black rather than a darker version of the original purple.
It is also the honest rescue for a bath that went brown. A brown you did not want becomes a charcoal you did. See [keeping a bark bath purple instead of brown](/blog/keeping-a-bark-bath-purple).
## Quantities

| Iron as % of dry fibre weight | Result |
| --- | --- |
| 0.5% | A slight cooling, barely visible |
| 1 to 2% | Slate, charcoal — the useful range |
| 4% and above | Near-black, and the wool starts to feel harsh |

Iron at strength weakens wool and silk over time, which is why historic iron-blacks are often the first parts of an old textile to fail. One to two per cent is where the colour is worth having and the fibre is not.
## Method

1. **A separate pot.** Iron contaminates: once a pot has held it, every pale bath afterwards comes out dulled. Mark the pot and keep it for this.
2. **Dissolve it fully** in hot water, in the pot, before the fibre goes near it.
3. **Dip, do not simmer.** Warm water, thirty seconds to a few minutes, moving the fibre continuously.
4. **Lift it early.** It reads two shades darker when dry than it looks wet.
5. **Rinse well**, then wash with a pH-neutral detergent. Iron left in the fibre keeps working.
## Partial dipping

Because the reaction is so quick, dipping only part of a skein gives a clean gradient in one pass — the base colour at one end, charcoal at the other. Hold the skein above the pot and lower it in stages, a minute apart.
## Handling
Iron sulfate stains everything it touches, including grout, counters and the pot you forgot to label. Work over a tray, and keep it out of reach of children and animals.

title: Wool, Silk, Cotton and Linen in the Same Bath
summary: Protein fibres and plant fibres take this colour very differently. Wool and silk go deep with alum alone; cotton and linen need a tannin step and two alum baths and still land paler and browner. Dyeing them together always disappoints one of them.
body: The same pot, the same day, the same liquid — and a wool skein comes out aubergine while the cotton beside it comes out milky tan. Nothing went wrong. They are different materials.
## Why they differ
**Protein fibres** — wool, silk, alpaca, mohair — are made of chains with plenty of sites a tannin-mordant complex can bond to. They take this colour readily and deeply.
**Cellulose fibres** — cotton, linen, hemp, ramie — are chains of sugar with far fewer such sites. Alum alone barely holds, which is why so many first attempts on a cotton shirt wash out to nothing.
## What each needs

| Step | Wool and silk | Cotton and linen |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Scour | Hot water, neutral detergent | Hot wash; linen benefits from a soda ash boil |
| Mordant | Alum at 10 to 15% | Tannin, then alum, then alum again |
| Bath temperature | About 80°C / 175°F | Up to 90°C / 195°F is fine |
| Handling | No agitation — it felts | Agitate freely |
| Result to expect | Deep purple to maroon | Muted mauve, tan, warm brown |

The three-step cellulose sequence is the whole difference. Tannin first gives the fibre something to hold; alum after it fixes that; a second alum bath deepens it further. Skipping it is the commonest cause of a cotton piece that looked fine wet and pale after one wash.
## Temperature, and why not to mix

Wool cannot go above about 80°C without risking felting, and it must not be agitated at temperature. Linen is happier hotter and does not care how much you stir it. A bath that suits one is the wrong bath for the other, which is why mixed-fibre dyeing ends in a compromise neither fibre wanted.

If you must dye both from one batch of bark, dye the wool first at its own temperature, then run the cotton through the [second bath](/blog/getting-a-second-and-third-bath-from-one-batch) hotter and for longer.
## Blends
A wool-cotton blend takes colour on the wool and much less on the cotton, which reads as a heather rather than a solid. That can be the point. Just decide it deliberately rather than discovering it.

title: Getting a Second and Third Bath From One Batch
summary: Spent bark still holds colour. A second bath typically gives a shade or two lighter than the first and a third lighter again, which is how a graded set of skeins comes from one batch. Keep the material wet between baths and use it within a few days.
body: A first bath takes the most easily released colour and leaves a good deal behind. Treating what is left as waste is the most expensive habit in this craft.
## What to expect from each pass

| Bath | Relative depth | Typical use |
| --- | --- | --- |
| First | Full | The deep skein |
| Second | Roughly half to two thirds | The mid shade of a graded set |
| Third | A quarter or less | Tints, cotton, blending fibre |
| Fourth | Little worth the fuel | Water the compost with it |
This is the cheapest way to dye a **gradient set**: three or four skeins from the same batch, each a step lighter, which match each other in a way separately mixed baths never quite do.
## Method

1. Lift the fibre out of the first bath when it is where you want it.
2. Keep the bark — in its mesh bag, or strained and returned to the pot.
3. Top the pot up with fresh water, bring it back to about 80°C, and hold it for an hour to load the new bath.
4. Enter the next fibre.
Going slightly longer and slightly hotter on later baths recovers more of what is left, and the browning risk is lower on a weaker bath than on a strong one.
## Storing between baths

Wet bark left warm goes off quickly, and a bath that smells sour will also dye unevenly. Keep the material submerged in cool water in a lidded bucket, in the coolest place you have, and use it within two or three days. Dried-out bark that has been wet once rarely gives much on a later pass.
A bath itself keeps about the same length of time. Smell it before you commit fibre to it.
## Which cut re-baths better

Shredded and stripped material has more still to give on a second pass, because the first bath only reached the outer surfaces. Powder gives up most of its colour to the first bath, so its second is weaker. See [the three cuts of mimosa root bark](/blog/the-three-cuts-of-mimosa-root-bark).
